market: Will Republicans lose the Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas Senate seats?
thesis: The YES outcome requires Republicans to lose all seven seats; it is an intersection, so its probability is bounded by the least likely Democratic win and pulled down by any race where the Republican still leads. Polling signal favors Democrats in six of seven races: Peltola +2 in Alaska, Hamilton +3.5 in Kansas, Jackson +4 in Maine, El-Sayed +7 in Michigan, Brown +5 in Ohio, Talarico +4.2 in Texas — consistent with a Democratic-leaning national environment, which is the real driver of a sweep scenario. The weakest link is Iowa: the latest poll has Republican Hinson ahead 47-46 and CBS classifies both Iowa and Kansas as Republican-leaning, so the joint event likely hinges on a race that is at best a coin flip for Democrats. Because a shared national environment correlates these races, the sweep probability is higher than the naive product of seven independent ~50% events (~1%), but the Iowa deficit and the red-state fundamentals of Alaska, Kansas, and Texas keep it in the low single digits with 3 days to the election. Single polls per race are anchors, not distributions; several of these leads are within typical polling error, which cuts against YES since YES needs every lead to hold simultaneously.

market: Will the Democratic Party win the NC-13 House seat?
thesis: Republican incumbent Brad Knott won this district by more than 70,000 votes in 2024, a landslide margin that places NC-13 deep in safe-Republican territory; seats of this type flip only a few percent of the time cycle-over-cycle. Knott is the incumbent in 2026, adding incumbency advantage on top of the district's partisan lean. The district's recent history shows some two-party competitiveness — a Democrat (Wiley Nickel) won it narrowly in 2022 — so this is not a permanently safe seat, but the 2024 map clearly favors Republicans. No public polling exists for this race, so there is no signal of an upset; absence of polling in a race this close to Election Day is itself consistent with forecasters and parties treating it as non-competitive. A 2026 midterm environment potentially favorable to Democrats (typical out-party midterm dynamics) is the main reason the probability is not lower, but a wave would need to be historically large to erase a 70,000-vote margin in four days.
falsifier: A late-breaking poll, forecasting-model update, or election-eve reporting showing Paul Barringer within single digits of Brad Knott would push this estimate up substantially.

thesis: The base rate from the last five Ohio Senate elections gives Democrats a 40% historical win rate in the state (f6). The election has not yet occurred and is scheduled for November 3, 2026, leaving roughly two days for late shifts, turnout effects, and polling error; a sub-1-point polling lead this close is consistent with either outcome (f1, f5). market: Will the Republican Party hold below 190 House seats after the 2026 midterm elections?
thesis: The Republican Party, as the president's party, enters the midterm with a historically high probability of losing seats (18 out of 20 midterms). To resolve YES, Republicans must lose at least 29 seats from their current 218. This is a very large loss, exceeding the historical average midterm loss of 27 seats for the president's party. A loss of 29 or more seats constitutes a 'wave' election. While possible, such a large loss is significantly less likely than a more modest loss consistent with the historical average. Given the extremely low probability of the required seat swing, the probability of the Republican Party holding below 190 seats is minimal.
falsifier: Widespread and reliable polling data indicating a catastrophic, unprecedented collapse in support for the Republican party just before the election.

market: Jaguars vs. Ravens
thesis: Baltimore's starting QB Lamar Jackson is out (thumb surgery, injured reserve) and backup Tyler Huntley left the last game with a toe injury and did not return; a team likely down to its third-string quarterback is a major downgrade well beyond the generic road-favorite case. Form signal favors Jacksonville: 5–2 record coming off a 35-point win, versus Baltimore at 4–4 coming off a 26-point home loss to Buffalo; both results point the same direction and are real signal, not just narrative. Counterweights keeping this below ~75%: the game is in Baltimore (home field is worth roughly 2–3 points), it is a short-week Thursday game which compresses preparation and adds variance, Huntley's status for Thursday is unresolved (he could play), and Jacksonville's Jakobi Meyers is questionable. The spread-cover base rate (f15) is only an anchor; moneyline outcomes for road favorites with a large QB edge historically run higher than the cover rate implies, justifying the upward adjustment from 62% to ~71%.
falsifier: Confirmation before Thursday that Tyler Huntley is fully cleared and starting, coupled with bad Jacksonville injury news, would move my estimate down toward 60%; conversely Baltimore announcing a third-string starter would push it toward 78%.

market: Jobless claims wk Nov 7: at least 180,000
thesis: Initial jobless claims (DOL advance SA figure), week ending Nov 7, 2026. Median estimate 192000. Base rate: Over 14 weeks advance prints ranged 189k-209k with mean absolute week-to-week change of about 3.1k, and actuals came in below the Econoday consensus 12 of 14 times (mean miss -3.6k), so the 195k consensus maps to roughly 191-192k centered on a prior print of 189k (likely revised to about 190k). The week ending Nov 7 carries a large seasonal-factor jump (about +8-11% NSA expected), and in comparable weeks the SA change was small and negative (2024 election week -4k and 7k under consensus with a ~10% factor jump; 2023 -3k; 2025 -1k), so the big factor jump has not produced upside surprises. Election Day is in the reference week but is not a filing holiday, and Veterans Day falls in the following week, so the holiday distortion is not in play here. The trend is gently down (199, 194, 194, 189) but 189k is a 4-month low after an NSA drop that seasonals expected to rise, so some bounce back toward the 192-196k range is plausible. No fraud, strike, federal layoff, or hurricane shock is visible; the main extra uncertainty is the unseen Nov 7 seasonal factor, so tails are kept slightly wider than the recent change history implies, with a modestly fatter right tail. Claims likely stay near recent lows at about 192k, a bit below the 195k consensus, because forecasters have overestimated claims most weeks and this week's seasonal adjustment has not historically produced upside surprises.
falsifier: An advance print of 200k or higher would show that the 189k print was noise and the November seasonal factor is under-adjusting, breaking the below-consensus pattern.

market: Existing home sales Oct: above 3.70M
thesis: NAR existing-home sales, Oct 2026, SAAR first print. Median estimate 3.85. Base rate: In Jan-Sep 2026 the first-reported monthly change was usually within 0.15M (8 of 9 months), revisions to the prior month averaged about +0.01M, and misses against consensus averaged about 0.05-0.06M, so a no-information prior is roughly 3.99 +/- 0.10. September pending home sales fell 7.3% to a record low with declines in every region, and contracts signed in September (rates at 6.95-7.03%, then above 7.2% in early October) close mostly in October-November; in past rate-shock episodes (Sep 2022, Aug 2023) a PHSI drop of this size flowed through as about a 2-6% drop in closings spread over the next two months. MBA purchase apps down 16-19% on the year, Redfin pendings at record lows, and a small Hurricane Isaias drag in the Florida Panhandle all point the same way, and the only named preview (Continuum) expects -3.3%, or about 3.86. August pendings were flat, which cushions part of October, so I center on a drop of about 3.5% to 3.85 and keep a fatter left tail. The record September drop in pending sales and the rate spike above 7% should pull October existing-home sales down about 3-4% from 3.99 to roughly 3.85M, the lowest in about 16 years.
falsifier: A print at or above 3.95 would show the September pending collapse was noise or slipped mostly into November, not October.
